name: Clean Air Task Force (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of greenhouse gas kept out of the air spares people everywhere (heat deaths), so the result is spread by world population; the small US power-plant smoke share is left in the world figure.
summary: Clean Air Task Force (Boston, with offices in Europe and Africa) advocates and does research for climate policy: methane rules, carbon capture, advanced nuclear and fusion energy, power plants and clean fuels; this model counts the six largest policies it worked on that were won in 2022-2025 (the EU Methane Regulation, EPA's oil and gas methane rule, the Inflation Reduction Act's carbon-capture credit, EPA's power-plant standards, the ADVANCE Act and fusion's regulatory framework) against its spending over those years ($42.96M in 2025). At the defaults a dollar given averts about 0.015 tonnes of CO₂e (about $68 a tonne), 0.0065 years of healthy life per $1,000, nearly all of it from the two methane rules, whose tonnes count for their heat deaths and for the ozone methane forms; it is low because each win is shared with many groups and with what governments would have done anyway (Clean Air Task Force is credited with 1% to 6% of each win), and the US rules have since been weakened or repealed. The biggest uncertainties are the shared discount rate and years a won reform counts, methane's ozone deaths per tonne, and how much of each win was advocacy's doing; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no tonne is measured for its work.

rows.label: Fusion: power deployed in its first decades, relative to the advanced-nuclear pathway
rows.explainer: Fusion line. If fusion works commercially, how much it would be built in its first decades, against DOE's 200 GW advanced-nuclear pathway as the yardstick for a new firm clean power source. Our judgment, half (0.1 to 1): fusion would start later and from a smaller supply chain; Clean Air Task Force's fusion work is international, which the yardstick doesn't count. Reference class: the advanced-nuclear pathway itself, a firm clean source starting about two decades earlier.

Share of each win due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won policy that is the advocates' doing rather than what governments, industry and events would have done at the same time. Every win below takes it; Clean Air Task Force's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row. The wins are in, so this is not a chance of winning.

Discounted years of impact (rules and tax credits)
rows.explainer: Read by the EPA methane, power-plant and carbon-capture branches.

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: years from the win until the import tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The regulation entered into force in August 2024; importers report from 2025 and the methane-intensity limit was to apply from August 2030. The Commission proposed in October 2026 (COM(2026) 569) to move it to August 2031; the Council backs one year's delay, the European Parliament three. Our judgment, 7 years from 2024 (6 to 10).

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: discounted years of impact
Advanced nuclear: share of DOE's pathway that gets built
rows.explainer: DOE's 200 GW is what liftoff would take, not a forecast: in 2026 no advanced reactor runs commercially in the US, and utilities remain reluctant to pay for first plants. Reference class: the last US build wave, where more than 100 reactor orders of the 1970s were cancelled, and Vogtle 3 and 4 (2023-2024), the only new US reactors in three decades, came seven years late and at more than twice the budget. Our judgment, 30% (10% to 70%), against the recent pull from data-centre demand and the 2024-2025 laws and orders backing it.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: share of that deployment due to the period's policy wins
rows.explainer: The wins Clean Air Task Force worked on in 2022-2025: the ADVANCE Act (signed July 2024: faster, cheaper licensing at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission), the COP28 and COP29 pledges to triple nuclear capacity, state laws lifting nuclear moratoria. Deployment turns mostly on cost, finance and demand; licensing is one of several barriers. Our judgment, 5% (1% to 15%) of the deployment.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: years until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The shared wait for a technology not yet deployed (facts: climate, 15 years, 8 to 25), anchored on DOE's ramp from 2030 to 2050.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: discounted years of impact
Fusion: chance it becomes a commercial power source by the 2050s
rows.explainer: One event: no fusion device has yet put net electricity on a grid. Reference class: fusion's own record of dates slipping (ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, now in the 2030s) against over 40 private companies aiming for pilot plants in the 2030s and the 2022 ignition result at the National Ignition Facility. Our judgment, 15% (3% to 40%), drawn as happens or doesn't (normalization.md 2.18).

rows.label: Fusion: share of its deployment due to the period's regulatory wins
rows.explainer: The wins Clean Air Task Force worked on: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's 2023 decision to regulate fusion machines like particle accelerators rather than fission reactors, written into the ADVANCE Act in 2024, and similar frameworks in the UK and elsewhere. A light, early framework saves years of licensing, but physics and cost decide most. Our judgment, 5% (1% to 15%), as for advanced nuclear.

rows.label: Fusion: extra years of waiting beyond a technology nearer market
rows.explainer: Fusion is further from market than advanced nuclear: first commercial plants in the late 2030s at best, deployment at scale in the 2040s and 2050s. Our judgment, 10 more years (3 to 20) than the shared technology wait.

rows.label: Fusion: years until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The shared technology wait (15 years) plus fusion's extra years: 25 at the defaults.

rows.label: Fusion: discounted years of impact

rows.formula: (eumr_downstream + usmeth_downstream + pwr_downstream + ccs_downstream + nuc_downstream + fus_downstream) / period_years
rows.explainer: The six wins of 2022-2025, each its tonnes a year × the advocacy share × its discounted years (× deployment and policy shares for the technologies), summed and spread over the period's years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the regulators' and modellers' tonnes should be trusted
rows.explainer: The tonnes are ex-ante estimates by the regulators (EPA) and modellers (Oeko-Institut, DOE, the shared judgment on the capture credit), not measured cuts. Regulators' estimates of a rule's cuts are sometimes too high (compliance short of the rule) and sometimes too low (methane leaks larger than inventories say); 2022's capture projections ran far ahead of what was built. Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), applied to every branch; delivery and repeal are in each branch's implementation row, not here.

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Share of the import cut that is real abatement, not trade reshuffled or counted elsewhere. Oeko-Institut holds trade constant, but exporters can send their cleanest, certified cargoes to Europe and the rest elsewhere: comparing with Rystad's trade-adjusted figures it finds a diversion potential of about a third of import methane (p. 29), and argues that spillovers to producers' practice limit the leakage (p. 32), so about 54% of the 110 Mt is real. US gas is about an eighth of the cut (p. 4) and the EPA rule's delivered share of it (80% × 40%) is already in the US methane branch: −4%. 54% × 0.96 = 52%. Our judgment, half (20% to 85%).

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Clean Air Task Force's share of all advocacy resources behind the regulation. It ran one of the largest European methane teams, worked with the Commission and the IEA on the import rules, and claims the regulation is in force 'thanks in part' to its advocacy (2024 Impact Report); the Environmental Defense Fund, Bellona, ECOS, the Environmental Investigation Agency and others campaigned too, and industry lobbied on both sides. On resources: its methane line was $5.1M in 2024, worldwide; the other groups' European methane work and the industry associations lobbying on the file (oil and gas producers, importers, utilities) were together several times that. Our judgment, 20% (8% to 40%): one of a handful of NGOs that worked the file full-time, against a much larger total. The share is Clean Air Task Force's own: its related lobbying organisation, CATF Action (a 501(c)(4), outside these accounts), is counted among the others.

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the win (Convention 2); it applies whichever way credit is shared, since no evaluator's other split is used.

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Share of the import standard's cut delivered: the methane-intensity limit is not yet set, the Commission proposed more flexibility in 2026 (COM(2026) 569) and a one-year delay was announced; gas-security pressure since 2022 weighs against a strict limit. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 90%).

rows.label: EPA methane rule: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Share of EPA's estimate that wouldn't have happened anyway: EPA's baseline already holds state rules; some operators cut leaks voluntarily (the Oil and Gas Methane Partnership, company pledges) and would have done more. Our judgment, 80% (60% to 100%).

rows.label: EPA methane rule: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the rule: it has worked on oil and gas methane since 2014 (rule designs, emissions studies, litigation: in 2024 it helped defeat stays in the D.C. Circuit and the Supreme Court), but the Environmental Defense Fund, much larger, led the field, beside NRDC, Earthjustice, Sierra Club and many state groups. On resources: Clean Air Task Force's whole methane line ($5.1M in 2024, worldwide) is a fraction of the Environmental Defense Fund's methane work (it built and launched its own methane-measuring satellite, MethaneSAT, in 2024), and industry's lobbying against parts of the rule was larger still. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%). The share is Clean Air Task Force's own: its related lobbying organisation, CATF Action (a 501(c)(4), outside these accounts), is counted among the others.

rows.label: EPA methane rule: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the win (Convention 2); it applies whichever way credit is shared, since no evaluator's other split is used.

rows.label: EPA methane rule: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Share of the rule's tonnes delivered: since 2025 EPA has pushed most compliance dates to January 2027, loosened flare and vent rules (April 2026) and proposed rescinding the super-emitter programme (October 2026); the rule still stands and is defended in court, and could be restored by a later administration within the years counted. Our judgment, 40% (15% to 70%).

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Share of EPA's estimate that wouldn't have happened anyway: coal plants were already closing for cost reasons; EPA's baseline includes the Inflation Reduction Act. Our judgment, 80% (50% to 100%).

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the standards: it says they reflect its policy design and defended them in court, among many groups (NRDC, Sierra Club, Earthjustice, EDF and states). Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%). The share is Clean Air Task Force's own: its related lobbying organisation, CATF Action (a 501(c)(4), outside these accounts), is counted among the others.

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the win (Convention 2); it applies whichever way credit is shared, since no evaluator's other split is used.

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Share of the standards' tonnes delivered: EPA repealed the existing-coal guidelines and the carbon-capture standards in September 2026 (effective 16 November 2026) and proposed repealing the rest, after rescinding the 2009 endangerment finding in February 2026. What remains is the chance courts or a later administration restore them within the years counted. Our judgment, 5% (1% to 20%).

rows.label: Carbon-capture credit: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Share of the stored tonnes that are real cuts: a few capture projects sit on plants or factories that would otherwise have closed or cut emissions some other way. The tonnes are already only those due to the larger credit. Our judgment, 90% (70% to 100%).

rows.label: Carbon-capture credit: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Clean Air Task Force's share of the resources behind the larger credit: a long-standing member of the Carbon Capture Coalition and an author of credit designs, inside a coalition of over 100 companies, unions and groups and a law moved by far larger forces. Our judgment, 3% (1% to 10%). The share is Clean Air Task Force's own: its related lobbying organisation, CATF Action (a 501(c)(4), outside these accounts), is counted among the others.

rows.label: Carbon-capture credit: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the win (Convention 2); it applies whichever way credit is shared, since no evaluator's other split is used.

rows.label: Carbon-capture credit: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Share of the credit's tonnes delivered: the 2025 budget law kept 45Q (and gave stored and used carbon the same rate) while cutting most other clean-energy credits; projects still face permits for wells and pipelines. Our judgment, 85% (60% to 95%).

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: the grid it joins, relative to today's US average intensity
rows.explainer: The grid intensity above (0.366 tonnes per MWh, today's US average) already averages in clean power, so this is only how much cleaner the grid a new reactor joins will be by the 2040s: renewables keep growing, coal keeps closing. Our judgment, 70% (40% to 100%) of today's average.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the period's nuclear wins: it has argued for advanced nuclear since 2007 and supported the ADVANCE Act and the tripling pledges, beside the Nuclear Energy Institute (the industry's lobby, far larger), ClearPath, Third Way, the Breakthrough Institute and reactor companies. Our judgment, 8% (3% to 20%). The share is Clean Air Task Force's own: its related lobbying organisation, CATF Action (a 501(c)(4), outside these accounts), is counted among the others.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the win (Convention 2); it applies whichever way credit is shared, since no evaluator's other split is used.

rows.label: Advanced nuclear: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Share of the wins that stands: the ADVANCE Act passed with large majorities in both parties and nuclear support has grown since. Our judgment, 95% (80% to 100%).

rows.label: Fusion: the grid it joins, relative to today's US average intensity
rows.explainer: As for advanced nuclear, how much cleaner the grid fusion joins will be than today's US average, which the tonnes already use; fusion comes later, so lower: 60% (30% to 100%), our judgment.

rows.label: Fusion: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: Clean Air Task Force's share of the advocacy resources behind fusion's regulatory frameworks: one of few non-profits working on them, beside the Fusion Industry Association and the companies themselves. Our judgment, 12% (4% to 30%). The share is Clean Air Task Force's own: its related lobbying organisation, CATF Action (a 501(c)(4), outside these accounts), is counted among the others.

rows.label: Fusion: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the win (Convention 2); it applies whichever way credit is shared, since no evaluator's other split is used.

rows.label: Fusion: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: Share of the frameworks that stands: the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's approach is written into law (ADVANCE Act) and has support in both parties. Our judgment, 95% (80% to 100%).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no tonne is measured for Clean Air Task Force's work. The tonnes are regulators' and modellers' estimates of whole policies, and its part in them a judgment. Every branch takes it.

rows.explainer: The branches' own rows apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's tonnes after the counterfactual and credit, for reading only.

rows.label: Other wins of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: The six wins are the period's largest, but much of the work isn't in them: the EU Methane Regulation's rules on Europe's own oil, gas and coal; the Fossil Fuel Regulatory Programme (methane rules with up to 20 low- and middle-income countries, from 2024); agricultural and waste methane; hydrogen and zero-carbon fuels rules; superhot-rock geothermal; US state laws; energy access in Africa; the defence of the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 30% of the modelled value (10% to 70%), below the roughly two-fifths of spending they take because the modelled wins are the biggest.

rows.label: Side effect: smog and toxic air pollution cut by the methane rules, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: EPA's methane rule also cuts smog-forming volatile organic compounds near wells: EPA's analysis gives about 56 (2028) to 74 (2038) ozone deaths a year avoided from them (Tables 3-8 and 3-9). Valued like other air-pollution deaths at the shared rates, that is about an eighth of the US methane branch, about +3.5% of the model's value (1.5% to 7%). These are local deaths from the rule's other pollutants, apart from methane's own worldwide ozone in extra_deaths_per_tco2e.

source.title: US EPA (2023), Regulatory Impact Analysis for the final oil and natural gas standards

rows.label: Side effect: extra oil from captured CO₂ used to push oil out of old wells, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Part of the CO₂ captured under 45Q is used for enhanced oil recovery, which keeps old fields producing; the 2025 law gave that use the full credit. The extra oil burned offsets part of the stored tonnes, a harm against the capture branch's small share of the value. Our judgment, −1% (−4% to 0).

rows.label: Side effect: accident, waste and proliferation risk from more reactors, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Nuclear power's deaths per unit of electricity, accidents and waste included, are about as low as wind's and solar's and far below fossil fuels' (Markandya & Wilkinson 2007); proliferation risk is small for reactors in the US. Our judgment, −0.2% of the modelled value (−1% to 0).

rows.label: All adjustments combined (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (eumr_downstream * eumr_total_adj + usmeth_downstream * usmeth_total_adj + pwr_downstream * pwr_total_adj + ccs_downstream * ccs_total_adj + nuc_downstream * nuc_total_adj + fus_downstream * fus_total_adj) / (eumr_downstream + usmeth_downstream + pwr_downstream + ccs_downstream + nuc_downstream + fus_downstream)
rows.explainer: The branches' own combined adjustments apply; this is their average, weighted by each branch's expected tonnes before adjustments, for reading only.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.formula: (eumr_expected_tonnes + usmeth_expected_tonnes) / (eumr_expected_tonnes + usmeth_expected_tonnes + pwr_expected_tonnes + ccs_expected_tonnes + nuc_expected_tonnes + fus_expected_tonnes)
rows.explainer: The two methane rules' share of the expected tonnes, weighted like the fuel share (before waits and years counted, which can't feed a conversion row).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.formula: (pwr_expected_tonnes + nuc_expected_tonnes + fus_expected_tonnes) / (eumr_expected_tonnes + usmeth_expected_tonnes + pwr_expected_tonnes + ccs_expected_tonnes + nuc_expected_tonnes + fus_expected_tonnes)
rows.explainer: Methane kept in pipes and wells carries no fuel smoke (its ozone is the row below), nor does CO₂ captured at a running plant; power-plant standards and new reactors cut US power plants' burning of coal and gas. The share is weighted by each win's expected tonnes a year once in effect (the waits and the shared years counted can't feed a conversion row, docs/normalization.md 2.5), so it slightly overweights the later technology tonnes; the smoke factor is so small that this barely moves the result.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of these fuel tonnes, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Per fuel and place: the power-plant standards' tonnes are coal plants' (facts: climate.us_coal_power_smoke_factor, 0.067 of the world average, from EPA's own analysis of the rule); new reactors and fusion displace the US power mix (climate.us_power_smoke_factor, 0.013). Weighted by each branch's expected tonnes; fusion's later tonnes may come anywhere, the US figure stands in.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tco2e unit's conversion (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Ozone deaths averted per tonne, from the methane in these tonnes
rows.explainer: Methane forms ground-level ozone worldwide within about a decade: the shared figure (facts: climate.ozone_deaths_per_tco2e_methane, 0.16 per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂e of methane, 0.05 to 0.48) times the methane share. The conversion values these deaths like other air-pollution deaths, undiscounted for their short wait. Methane's heat deaths go through the shared conversion like CO₂'s (a 60-year delay and GWP100): methane warms within one to two decades, so that understates them at a high discount rate and overstates them at a low one; a separate methane delay would be a change to the shared conversion, not this model.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per year of the period
rows.formula: (eumr_downstream * eumr_total_adj + usmeth_downstream * usmeth_total_adj + pwr_downstream * pwr_total_adj + ccs_downstream * ccs_total_adj + nuc_downstream * nuc_total_adj + fus_downstream * fus_total_adj) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj + voc_health_share + eor_oil_share + nuclear_harm_share)
rows.explainer: Each win's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed, spread over the period's four years, with the other wins and the side effects added as shares.
